值得閱讀的理由

  • 從男性精子品質、女性凍卵到胚胎基因篩選，了解科技如何改變生育準備與選擇。
  • 拆解多基因胚胎篩檢的原理、商業推力與科學限制，避免把預測結果誤當成確定答案。
  • 透過當事父母與作者的經歷，看見生育科技背後的焦慮、倫理爭議與漫長等待。

摘要

生育焦慮與「卵子最大化」

台灣生育率低迷，不只反映有人選擇不生，也掩蓋了許多人想要孩子、卻難以順利懷孕的處境。有人尋求試管嬰兒、捐卵或捐精，也有人跨國尋找代理孕母；而在美國矽谷，部分人更試圖把生育推向極限，想在胚胎植入前比較基因，挑選理想中的孩子。

三十歲的康納得知妻子自然受孕不易後，開始研究如何改善精子品質，少喝酒、改穿寬鬆內褲、避免手機放在口袋，並服用營養補充品。網路上甚至有人以冰水浸泡睪丸，希望增加精子生成；但即使後來成功懷孕，也難以確認究竟是哪種方法發揮作用。與此同時，矽谷一個名為「Egg Rolling」的女性社群，成員致力於反覆取卵、累積數十甚至數百顆卵子，這種做法被稱為「卵子最大化」，有些人希望藉此保留生育機會，有些人則想日後培養更多胚胎並進行基因篩選。

胚胎也能像商品一樣比較？

這些準備背後有現實因素：研究估計，全球男性平均精子濃度在1973至2018年間下降約52%；女性的卵子儲備則會隨年齡增加而減少，卵子染色體異常的機率也會上升。晚婚晚育日益普遍，使不少女性希望趁年輕多保存卵子。

《紐約》雜誌報導的亞瑟與查斯，計畫透過捐卵及代理孕母生育，並使用基因公司 Genomic Prediction 評估胚胎未來的智商、身高，以及心臟病、糖尿病等疾病風險，服務費用高達約新台幣164萬元。他們從30顆成熟卵子開始，經過培養與檢測，最後留下三個染色體正常的胚胎。由於預測的智商與身高差異不大，兩人主要依據疾病風險作出選擇。生孩子似乎從祈求平安出生，變成能逐項比較條件的決策。

技術進步、商業化與生育觀念

胚胎篩選熱潮有三個推力。第一是基因技術進步：傳統胚胎著床前檢測能檢查特定遺傳疾病或染色體異常；新興的多基因胚胎篩檢則利用大型基因資料庫與統計模型，估算多種基因變異與疾病風險、身高等特徵的關聯。Genomic Prediction 會提供胚胎比較報告，Nucleus Genomics 甚至設計出類似網購介面的工具，讓使用者排序不同特徵。

第二是生殖醫療逐漸成為高價、客製化服務。Genomic Prediction 曾在紐約地鐵刊登「打造最好的寶寶」廣告，並吸引約三千人登記等候。部分父母不願把孩子的健康交給運氣，希望取得更多基因資訊；若未來能以人體細胞在實驗室大量製造卵子，可供篩選的胚胎還可能更多。

第三是生育理念的轉變。矽谷的鼓勵生育思潮常強調傳承優良基因，但不少父母並非想生很多孩子，而是認為既然能用科技降低疾病風險，就值得一試。只是降低遺傳疾病風險與挑選智商、身高或壽命，牽涉不同層次的倫理問題。哈佛醫學院調查中，77%受訪者支持以胚胎篩檢降低特定身體疾病風險，支持藉此選擇身體特徵者則約為30%，顯示多數人追求的未必是完美寶寶。

預測的限制與父母的焦慮

多基因篩檢的效果仍有爭議。美國生殖醫學會指出，目前證據不足以證明這項技術具有可靠的臨床效益，因此不建議作為常規醫療服務。Genomic Prediction 曾宣稱經篩選的胚胎智商預測差距可能達九分，但這個比較前提是至少有20個可用胚胎；許多接受試管療程的父母，最後往往只有一兩個胚胎可供選擇。研究者也提醒，預測存在誤差，而不同多基因分數可能選出不同的「最佳」胚胎。科技公司所說的「最好」，並沒有科學界一致認定的標準。

然而，父母的焦慮是真實的。父親麥克斯與伴侶進行試管療程後，只得到兩個可用胚胎，基因分析顯示兩者預測壽命僅差五個月，他們仍決定再次接受療程，盼望有更多選擇。亞瑟的兒子出生後，他也因讀到高海拔環境可能影響神經發展的研究而擔憂，甚至考慮改變居住安排。

作者也分享了自身經驗：他們透過美國代理孕母迎來 Amo，從捐卵、試管嬰兒到胚胎篩檢，最後留下四個胚胎，並依基因檢測結果排序。然而，他們認為最理想的胚胎並未成功著床；歷經多次失敗，四年後才終於迎接孩子。這段經歷讓作者體會到，生殖科技能提供大量資訊，卻不能保證懷孕成功，也無法消除等待與不確定性。

================================================

It’s no longer news that Taiwan has the world's lowest fertility rate. While choosing not to have children is a personal decision, beyond economic issues, the low fertility rate also masks the reality that many people want to have children but are unable to do so successfully. Some people constantly seek help from in vitro fertilization and other assisted reproductive technologies to have children; some need egg donors or sperm donors, and others even have to cross borders to find surrogates to realize their dream of becoming parents. However, a more surprising trend has emerged in Silicon Valley, USA. There is a group of people who not only want to use technology to have children but also want to push their reproductive. capabilities to the limit, even hoping to compare and grade the genes of their future babies before deciding which one to choose. So, do they really get their wish and have a perfect baby? From high-tech gadgets to major revolutions, how particular are we about having children and conception today? There was a 30- year-old man, Connor, whose wife struggled to conceive for over a year. The doctor told him that natural conception was likely difficult. Connor was devastated upon hearing this and began obsessively researching how to improve the quality of his sperm and maximize his fertility. He started.

drinking less alcohol, switched to loose-fitting underwear, stopped keeping his phone in his pocket, and took various nutritional supplements. Online , some people even soak their testicles in ice water every day, believing it helps with sperm production. Some of these methods have scientific backing, while others do not. Even if Connor later successfully helped his wife conceive, there is no way to determine which measure actually worked. Women are not far behind. An investigation by The Information reporter this year found that there is a women's group in Silicon Valley called "Egg Rolling," with over 80 members, many of whom are high-level. tech professionals. What they study isn't how to "freeze eggs," but how to accumulate hundreds or even 200 eggs through repeated retrievals; this trend is called "egg maximization." Some women just want to preserve their future fertility, but others hope to create more embryos in the future and then use genetic technology to select the "ideal" one. It is actually quite common to spend so much energy on preparing for pregnancy. A study published in 2021 found that in the 45 years leading up to 2018, the average global male sperm concentration fell by.

an estimated 52%. Another Danish study also found that while the quantity of sperm from local donors did not decrease significantly, the total number of motile sperm dropped by 22%over three years. For women, the issue is more practical. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists points out that a woman's egg reserve steadily declines from birth, and as she gets older, the likelihood of chromosomal abnormalities in her eggs increases. Especially now that more and more people are marrying and having children later, it’s no wonder many women want to freeze more eggs while they are young to preserve their chances of having children in the future. Once the eggs. are ready, the next step is to maximize the embryos themselves. A couple interviewed by New York magazine this year, Arthur and Chas, did exactly that. Arthur, who previously worked at tech companies like Amazon and Twitter, is a massive data enthusiast. They hoped to have their own child through egg donation and a surrogate, but Arthur wanted to go further by using a company called Genomic Prediction to analyze the embryo’s future IQ, height, and risks for diseases like heart disease and diabetes. This service costs as much as 1.64 million New Taiwan Dollars. Starting with 30 mature eggs,.

they went through cultivation and testing, eventually leaving three embryos with normal chromosomes for further comparison. The predicted IQ and height for the three embryos were actually quite similar, so they ultimately based their choice mainly on disease risk. In the past, having a baby meant just hoping for a safe delivery, but now you can actually compare various criteria like shopping for goods; how exactly is this technology achieving this? And why are more and more people wanting to use it? There are three key drivers behind this wave of embryo maximization. , the first being the obvious advancement in genetic technology. With IVF in the past, doctors could use pre-implantation genetic testing to check for specific hereditary diseases or abnormal chromosome counts; for example, some severe single-gene disorders could be avoided with testing to help parents. Now, a technique called polygenic embryo screening has emerged. The concept is simple: conditions like diabetes, heart disease, or even height aren't determined by a single gene, but are influenced by many genes and environmental factors. So, scientists use large genetic databases to analyze.

the relationship between different genetic variants and diseases, then use statistical models to score embryos and predict their likely future traits and higher disease risks. Genomic Prediction can organize the genetic information of different embryos into a report for parents to compare. The magazine also discovered that another company, Nucleus Genomics, has even launched an interface that allows you to sort through various embryo traits, much like shopping for items online. The second driver is that reproductive medicine is starting to become a premium, customized commodity. Last year, Genomic Prediction ran large. advertisements in the New York subway boldly declaring, "Create your best baby ." Even though it sparked controversy, the result was that about 3,000 people signed up for the waitlist. Why are so many people willing to spend the money? A lab director at Genomic Prediction told NPR that some parents simply don't want to leave their child's health to chance and want as much genetic information as possible. Moreover, there is still significant room for this business to grow. If, in the future, scientists can truly mass-produce eggs in the lab using human cells, parents might not need to go through repeated egg retrievals and could obtain more.

embryos to screen. The third driver is a change in the philosophy of having children. We previously introduced the pro-natalism popular in Silicon Valley, where people like Elon Musk believe that superior genes should be passed on through more children. However, many parents don't want to have a dozen kids ; they just think if technology can reduce the risk of disease, why not give it a try? These two ways of thinking might seem similar, but they are actually backed by very different values . Using technology to reduce the risk of hereditary disease versus choosing a child's IQ, height, or lifespan are ethical issues on different levels. A poll by the Harvard Medical School found. that 77%of respondents support using embryo screening to reduce the risk of certain physical diseases. However, only about 30%of people support using it to select physical traits. This means that most people don't necessarily want a perfect baby; they just hope their children are... No. However, a major problem arises here : when tech companies tell you that spending money can result in a smarter, healthier child, are these predictions actually that accurate? First, it must be said that genetic testing does have.

significant medical value, especially for parents with a history of hereditary diseases; these technologies can help them lower the risk of having a child with a serious condition. But the efficacy of polygenic embryo screening remains highly controversial. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine clearly stated late last year that there is currently insufficient evidence to prove that this new screening technology has reliable clinical benefits, and therefore, it is not recommended as a routine medical service. New York Magazine also revealed that Genomic Prediction once claimed that the predicted IQ difference between screened embryos could be as much as nine points. However, that 前提 is that。you must first have 20 usable embryos to compare the highest and lowest scores. The problem is that many parents doing IVF end up with only one or two viable embryos. Geneticists point out that even with one embryo, the actual benefits of this technology may be limited, and the predictions themselves have margins of error. A 2024 study published in a Nature-affiliated journal found that using different polygenic scores can even result in selecting different " best" embryos due to varying criteria. So, if a tech company tells you they can use an algorithm to select the best baby , don't rush to pay up, because even scientists might not have a consensus on.

what "the best" actually means. However , what I think is worth considering is the genuine anxiety felt by these parents. Wired magazine interviewed a father named Max, who, after undergoing IVF with his partner, only ended up with two viable embryos. Genetic analysis showed a difference of only five months in predicted lifespan between the two, so they decided to go through IVF again , hoping for more options. As for Arthur , mentioned at the beginning, he was still worried after his son was born because he read a study suggesting that high-altitude environments might affect a child’s neurological development, and. he even considered changing the family’s living arrangements. This reminds me of our own experience. We welcomed Amo’s birth through surrogacy in the U.S. After egg donation, IVF, and embryo screening, we were left with four embryos. These embryos were ranked after genetic testing, but the one we thought was the best didn't result in a successful pregnancy. After several failures, it took us four years to finally welcome our child. This experience made me deeply realize that reproductive technology can provide a lot of information and help parents make choices, but it cannot guarantee.

the outcome. Of course, we want our children to be healthy, to have fewer illnesses and more opportunities—a sentiment every parent can understand— but that doesn’t mean we can truly use technology to determine who our children will become in the future. A science journalist interviewed by Vox reminded us that becoming a parent is fundamentally a process of learning to let go of control. Human genetics are too complex, and no matter how advanced technology becomes, it cannot dictate a child's entire life. Returning to Taiwan , beyond discussing how to increase birth rates, we should also look at whether those who want children but cannot conceive have sufficient medical. resources and institutional support. For some, having a child is a wish that can only be realized after a long and arduous journey. Whether it's IVF, donation, or surrogacy, different ways of having children shouldn't be seen as abnormal or unworthy of support just because they don't fit the traditional family mold. Technology should help us expand the possibilities of becoming parents, rather than ensuring that only the wealthy can access good reproductive choices. But we must remember that a child is not an investment, nor is a human being a product whose return on investment can be calculated. We can strive to give our children a better start in life, but we cannot demand that.

their lives conform to our predetermined standards. If one day you could pay to learn more about your child’s genetic information before they are born, how much would you want to know, and what price would you be willing to pay for such uncertainty? Feel free to leave your comments and share your thoughts. Great. Revolution.
